979.t: Song conquers Northern Han · Battle of the Gaoliang River
979.d: In 978 Wuyue and the Zhangzhou–Quanzhou regime surrendered their lands; in 979 Emperor Taizong of Song marched on Taiyuan in person, the Northern Han ruler Liu Jiyuan came out to surrender, and the division of the Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms ended. In the seventh month Taizong pressed on to attack Liao and was badly beaten at the Gaoliang River outside Youzhou; the Sixteen Prefectures were never recovered by the Song. Liao held the Sixteen Prefectures and the steppe south of the Gobi; the Tangut Dingnan Jun, the Guiyi Jun and the Ganzhou Uyghurs of Hexi, the Qocho Uyghurs of the Tian Shan and Khotan, and the Kara-Khanids and Samanids west of the Pamirs each went their own way. In the west the Buyids controlled the Abbasid caliph in Baghdad, the Fatimids held Egypt and southern Syria, Byzantium under Basil II was locked in a hard war with Samuel of Bulgaria, and Kievan Rus' was about to enter the reign of Grand Prince Volodymyr.

986.d: In 982 Li Jipeng of the Dingnan Jun surrendered the four prefectures of Xia, Sui, Yin and You to Song; his clansman Li Jiqian fled to Dijin Marsh and gathered the Tangut tribes to resist Song. Emperor Shengzong took the Liao throne under the regency of Empress Dowager Xiao, and in 985–986 Liao destroyed the state of Jeongan on the Yalu. In 986 Emperor Taizong of Song sent three columns north under Cao Bin, Tian Zhongjin and Pan Mei; Cao Bin's eastern army was crushed at Qigou Pass, and in the west Yang Ye, left without support, was trapped in Chenjia Valley, captured, and died for his country. From then on Song turned from attack to defense; in the twelfth month the Liao army came south and beat the Song army again at Junziguan. In Jiaozhou Lê Hoàn usurped the throne of the Đinh (980) and drove back the Song army at the Bạch Đằng River the next year. Grand Prince Volodymyr of Kyiv took Polotsk (980).

999.t: Fall of the Samanids · Rise of the Ghaznavids
999.d: In Zhidao 3 (997) Song divided the realm into fifteen circuits; that year Emperor Zhenzong took the throne, made Li Jiqian military governor of the Dingnan Jun and gave back the four prefectures of Xia, Sui, Yin and You, and the Tanguts grew strong. Liao took Yizhou in 989; in 999 Empress Dowager Xiao and Emperor Shengzong marched south, and Yang Yanzhao held Suicheng. West of the Pamirs the Samanid state fell into civil war: in 994 Sebüktigin of Ghazni helped the Samanids put down a revolt and took Khorasan; in 999 his son Mahmud formally took Khorasan, and in the same year the Kara-Khanids broke into Bukhara, the Samanids fell, and Transoxiana passed to the Turks. The Ma'munid dynasty united Khwarazm in 995. In the 990s Poland took Silesia, Lesser Poland and Moravia; Samuel of Bulgaria took the title of tsar and fought back and forth with Basil II of Byzantium.

1004.d: In 1001 Song divided Sichuan and the Gorges into the four circuits of Yi, Zi, Li and Kui. Li Jiqian took Lingzhou in 1002 and renamed it Xiping Fu; in 1004 he attacked Xiliang Fu, was shot in an ambush set by Panluozhi of the Six Valleys tribes and died, and his son Li Deming, who succeeded him, turned to Song. In the same year Empress Dowager Xiao and Emperor Shengzong of Liao marched south in force as far as Chanzhou; Kou Zhun urged Emperor Zhenzong to take the field in person, and the Song army shot dead the Liao vanguard commander Xiao Talin. In the twelfth month the Treaty of Chanyuan was concluded: Song would pay Liao 100,000 taels of silver and 200,000 bolts of silk a year, the two states would be "brothers", the border would follow the Baigou River, and there was no major war for more than a century. Liao built Zhenzhou (Kedun City) on the steppe north of the Gobi and garrisoned it to control the Zubu. Byzantium recovered the lower Danube and Skopje.

1019.t: Byzantium conquers Bulgaria · Victory at Gwiju
1019.d: In 1006 the Kara-Khanids destroyed Khotan, and the southern rim of the Tarim Basin became Muslim. In 1007 Emperor Shengzong of Liao built the Central Capital, Dading Fu, on the old land of the Xi king. In 1009 Lý Công Uẩn replaced the Lê and founded the Lý dynasty, moving the capital to Thăng Long the next year. In 1010 Emperor Shengzong invaded Goryeo in person and burned Gaegyeong; in 1018 Xiao Paiya invaded again and the next year was crushed by Gang Gam-chan at Gwiju (on the Cha and Tuo rivers), after which Liao and Goryeo made peace. In 1014 Basil II of Byzantium destroyed the main Bulgarian army at Kleidion and blinded 14,000 prisoners; by 1018 all Bulgaria had passed to Byzantium, and Basil II was called "the Bulgar-Slayer". Mahmud of Ghazni took Khwarazm in 1017 and campaigned east into India, taking Multan and Peshawar. The Ganzhou Uyghurs took Liangzhou in 1015.

1028.d: In 1023 Song divided Jiangnan into East and West circuits, making eighteen circuits. Li Deming submitted to both Song and Liao, and in 1020 built up Xingzhou (later Xingqing Fu) at Huaiyuan Town. In 1028 his son Li Yuanhao stormed Ganzhou; the khagan of the Ganzhou Uyghurs burned himself to death, and the Uyghur remnant fell back to Suzhou and later moved south to become the Yellow-headed Uyghurs. Mahmud of Ghazni took Lahore in 1021, raided Gujarat in 1025 and sacked the temple of Somnath, and in 1029 went west to take Rayy and imprison the Buyid ruler of Rayy. Byzantium annexed Vaspurakan in Armenia (1021). In 1024 Yaroslav the Wise and his brother divided the two banks of the Dnieper between them, and Rus' was for a time split in two.

1036.t: Xia takes the Hexi Corridor · Gusiluo's state founded
1036.d: Li Yuanhao succeeded in 1032 and took Liangzhou that year; in 1036 he took the Su, Gua and Sha prefectures as well, ending both the Guiyi Jun and the remnant of the Ganzhou Uyghurs, so that Western Xia held the whole Hexi Corridor; he also created the Tangut script. Gusiluo, a descendant of the Tibetan emperors, founded a state at Zongge and Qingtang (today's Xining), allied with Song against Xia, and crushed Yuanhao at Zongge in 1035. The brothers Tughril and Chaghri of the Seljuk clan of the Oghuz crossed the Amu Darya southward, defeated the Ghaznavid garrisons in Khorasan, and in 1036–1037 took Merv and Nishapur. The Byzantine general George Maniakes took Edessa in 1031.

1040.t: Li Yuanhao proclaims himself emperor · Battle of Dandanaqan
1040.d: In 1038 Li Yuanhao proclaimed himself emperor of the Great Xia, with his capital at Xingqing Fu; the Song called it Western Xia. In 1040 Yuanhao attacked Yanzhou and wiped out the forces of the Song generals Liu Ping and Shi Yuansun at Sanchuankou; Song sent Fan Zhongyan and Han Qi to take charge of Shaanxi and build forts. In the same year, at Dandanaqan near Merv, the Seljuk cavalry surrounded the great army of the Ghaznavid sultan Mas'ud for three days and won a great victory; the Ghaznavids withdrew from Khorasan for good, and the Seljuk empire was formally founded. In the early 1040s the Kara-Khanids split into eastern and western khanates.

1044.t: Treaty of Qingli · Battle of Hequ
1044.d: Western Xia beat the Song armies again at Haoshuichuan in 1041 and Dingchuan Fort in 1042, but was itself worn out by war and the closing of the border markets. In 1044 Song and Xia concluded the Treaty of Qingli: Yuanhao acknowledged himself a subject of Song, and Song each year "bestowed" silver, silk and tea totaling 255,000 units. That year Emperor Xingzong of Liao, accusing Xia of luring away Tangut subjects, led an army against Xia in person and was instead defeated by Yuanhao at Hequ (north of the Helan Mountains). Liao raised Yunzhou to the Western Capital, Datong Fu, and created the Western Capital Circuit, completing the five capitals. The Seljuks took Rayy in 1042 and Khwarazm in 1043 and pressed on west onto the Iranian plateau.

1055.t: Seljuks enter Baghdad · Rebellion of Nong Zhigao
1055.d: In 1045 Byzantium annexed Armenia and took Ani. The Seljuk Tughril took Isfahan in 1051, received the submission of the princes of Azerbaijan in 1054, and in 1055, at the caliph's call, entered Baghdad, overthrew the Buyid regime in Iraq and was named sultan, "King of the East and the West"; the Buyids were left with Fars alone. In 1048 a son of Chaghri set up a separate Seljuk branch in Kerman. In 1052 Nong Zhigao of Quảng Nguyên Châu rose against Song, took Yongzhou and swept down the river to besiege Guangzhou; in 1053 Di Qing seized Kunlun Pass in a night attack and crushed him. In 1048 the Yellow River broke through the Shanghu dike at Chanzhou and turned north, reaching the sea at Qianning Jun by way of Daming and Jizhou. In 1054 Jiaozhi took the name Đại Việt.

1071.d: Emperors Yingzong and Shenzong of Song succeeded in turn; Chong E took Suizhou in 1067 (later Suide Jun), and Wang Anshi's reforms began in 1069. The Seljuks took Fars in 1062, ending the Buyids; in 1064 Alp Arslan took Ani, and in August 1071, at Manzikert on the north shore of Lake Van, he crushed the Byzantine army and captured Emperor Romanos IV, after which the Turkish tribes poured into Asia Minor. In the same year the Norman Robert Guiscard took Bari, and Byzantium withdrew from Italy. In 1057 Anawrahta, king of Pagan in Burma, destroyed the Mon kingdom of Thaton. The Kipchaks (Cumans) poured onto the steppe north of the Black Sea from the east, and the remnant of the Oghuz moved west into the Balkans.

1077.t: Song expansion into Xihe · Song–Đại Việt war
1077.d: In 1072–1073 Wang Shao won over the Qingtang tribes and defeated Muzheng, recovering the Xi, He, Tao, Min, Dang and Die prefectures; Song set up the Xihe Circuit and extended its territory by over two thousand li. In the same year Song redivided the realm into twenty-three circuits. In 1075 the Đại Việt general Lý Thường Kiệt took the Qin, Lian and Yong prefectures and massacred Yongzhou; in 1076–1077 Guo Kui counterattacked as far as the Phú Lương River and withdrew after taking Quảng Nguyên Châu. In Asia Minor the Seljuk prince Suleiman founded the Sultanate of Rum, and the Danishmendids held Sivas and Kayseri; the Seljuk commander Atsiz took Jerusalem in 1073 and Damascus in 1076, and the Fatimids fell back to the coast.

1082.t: Five-pronged campaign against Xia · Defeat at Yongle
1082.d: In 1081 Empress Dowager Liang of Western Xia imprisoned Emperor Huizong; Emperor Shenzong of Song, "to call Xia to account", sent five columns against Xia. Li Xian took Lanzhou, and the columns of Liu Changzuo and Gao Zunyu converged on Lingzhou, but the Xia breached the Yellow River dikes to flood their camps and the Song army broke. In 1082 Song built Yongle in the Hengshan Range; 300,000 Xia troops besieged it and cut off its water, and the fort fell with the loss of over 200,000 Song soldiers and civilians; Shenzong wept at the news. The Rum sultan Suleiman took Nicaea as his capital in 1078–1081 and advanced to the Bosporus. Armenians in the mountains of Cilicia founded the Rubenid principality. In 1081 Alexios I of the Komnenian dynasty took the Byzantine throne and fought hard against the Normans at Dyrrhachium.

1092.d: In 1092 the Seljuk sultan Malik-Shah and his vizier Nizam al-Mulk were both assassinated; his sons fought over the throne, and the empire began to break up. Before this the Seljuks had taken Aleppo (1086), Antioch (1086) and Edessa (1087) and absorbed the Marwanids of Diyarbakır (1085), and the Western Kara-Khanids had submitted in 1089; Khwarazm was held hereditarily by the line of Anushtegin, a Turkish governor appointed by the Seljuks. In 1090 Hasan-i Sabbah seized Alamut Castle, and the Nizaris (the Assassins) rose. In 1091 Byzantium and the Cumans wiped out the Pechenegs at Levounion. Raška and Duklja in Serbia became independent. In Song the conservatives took power (the Yuanyou restoration).

1099.d: In 1095 Pope Urban II called for the crusade at Clermont. In 1097 the Crusaders helped Byzantium recover Nicaea and defeated the sultan of Rum at Dorylaeum; in 1098 they took Edessa and besieged and took Antioch, and in July 1099 they stormed Jerusalem and massacred its people. The Seljuks of Syria, split among the emirs of Aleppo, Damascus and other cities, could not come to the rescue. Emperor Zhezong of Song revived the New Policies and pressed on Xia by building forts: in 1098 Zhang Jie crushed the great army led in person by Empress Dowager Liang of Western Xia at Pingxia. In 1099 Song took Huizhou and, exploiting civil strife among Gusiluo's heirs, took Miaochuan and Qingtang, making them the prefectures of Huangzhou and Shanzhou. In Dali the powerful minister Gao Shengtai, who had usurped the throne, returned it to the Duan (1096); this is called the Later Dali.

1101.d: Emperor Zhezong of Song died in the first month of 1100 and his younger brother Huizong took the throne, with Empress Dowager Xiang acting as regent; the next year the era was renamed Jianzhong Jingguo, meant to reconcile the New Policies faction and its opponents. Judging Hehuang too isolated to hold, the court gave up Shanzhou in 1100 and Huangzhou in 1101, handing them back to Longza (Zhao Huaide) of Gusiluo's royal house; before long his younger brother Xisheluosa drove him out and took power. Emperor Daozong of Liao died in the first month of 1101 and was succeeded by his grandson, Emperor Tianzuo. In 1100 Baldwin I succeeded Godfrey and took the title King of Jerusalem; in 1101 a new wave of Crusaders arrived and was routed in Asia Minor by Rum and the Danishmendids, first at Mersivan and then at Heraclea.

1104.d: Cai Jing became chief minister in 1102 and renewed "frontier expansion": in 1103 Wang Hou and Tong Guan retook Huangzhou, and in the fourth month of 1104 they crushed Xisheluosa on the Zongge Plain; Shanzhou and Kuozhou surrendered one after the other, Shanzhou was renamed Xining Zhou, Gusiluo's state came to an end, and the Song frontier reached west to the east of Qinghai Lake. That winter Xisheluosa joined forces to press on Xuanwei City, and Western Xia raided Zhenrong Jun; in 1105 Song built Yinzhou City in the Hengshan Range, and in 1106, after Liao sent envoys asking on Xia's behalf for the occupied land to be returned, Song downgraded Yinzhou to a fort, Xia submitted a letter of apology, and the two sides stopped fighting. The Crusaders were defeated at Harran in 1104 and the count of Edessa was captured, but in the same year they took Acre. In 1102 Croatia made a pact with Hungary, whose king thereafter also ruled Croatia. The Danishmendids took Malatya in 1102.

1115.d: Aguda of the Wanyan clan of the Wild Jurchens succeeded in 1113 and rose against Liao in 1114, taking Ningjiang Zhou in the ninth month and crushing the Liao army at Chuhedian in the eleventh. In the first month of 1115 Aguda proclaimed himself emperor of the Great Jin, with his capital at Huining and the reign title Shouguo; in the eighth month he took Huanglong Fu; in the twelfth month Emperor Tianzuo of Liao marched east with a great army of 700,000, which Aguda met with 20,000 horsemen at Hubudagang and routed. The Crusaders took Tripoli in 1109 and founded the County of Tripoli. In 1117 the Seljuk sultan Sanjar set up Bahram-Shah as Ghaznavid ruler, and the Ghaznavids became Seljuk vassals.

1117.d: In 1116 Gao Yongchang, a junior officer at the Liao Eastern Capital, made himself independent at Liaoyang as the state of Great Balhae; the Jin army, invited to help, soon killed him and took the Eastern Capital, Liaoyang Fu, and more than fifty prefectures of Liaodong. In 1117 Jin took Changchun Zhou and Taizhou to the north, and all of northeastern Liao passed into Jin hands; Goryeo seized the chance to take the Liao prefecture of Bao (Uiju). Liao still held half its realm along the line of the Sixteen Prefectures and the Central Capital, and the Song court began to plan an alliance with Jin against Liao.

1120.t: Alliance Conducted at Sea · Jin takes the Supreme Capital
1120.d: From 1118 the Song envoy Ma Zheng and others sailed to Jin several times, and in 1120 the "Alliance Conducted at Sea" was concluded: Song and Jin would attack Liao together, Jin taking the Central Capital and Song taking Yanjing; once Liao was destroyed the Sixteen Prefectures would go to Song, and Song would pay Jin the annual payments it had made to Liao. In the fifth month of that year Aguda led the campaign in person and took the Liao Supreme Capital, Linhuang Fu, in a single day. In southeastern Song Fang La rose, sweeping through six prefectures and fifty-two counties of Liangzhe and Jiangdong, and Tong Guan led the troops meant for the northern campaign south to suppress him. The Seljuk empire split in two: Sanjar held Khorasan as Great Sultan, and the Seljuks of Iraq ruled western Iran and Mesopotamia from Hamadan (1118).

1122.d: In the first month of 1122 Jin took the Liao Central Capital and Emperor Tianzuo fled west to the Jiashan hills; in the third month Yelü Chun, custodian of Yanjing, was raised to the throne (the Northern Liao); in the fourth month Jin took the Western Capital as well. Song sent Tong Guan and Cai You with 150,000 troops against Yanjing, and in the fifth month they were beaten by Xiao Gan and Yelü Dashi at Baigou and Fancun. In the ninth month the Liao general Guo Yaoshi surrendered the Zhuo and Yi prefectures to Song; in the tenth month the Song general Liu Yanqing attacked Yanjing again, and Guo Yaoshi broke into the city but was routed when no reinforcements came. In the twelfth month Aguda entered Yanjing through Juyong Pass, and the Northern Liao came to an end. David IV "the Builder" of Georgia won the great victory of Didgori in 1121 and recovered Tbilisi in 1122.

1125.d: In 1123 Jin, as agreed, handed over Yanjing and the six prefectures of Zhuo, Yi, Tan, Shun, Jing and Ji to Song, which made the annual payments plus a "tax substitute" of a million strings of cash and renamed Yanjing as Yanshan Fu; Aguda died and was succeeded by his brother Wuqimai (Emperor Taizong of Jin). In 1124 Western Xia acknowledged itself a subject of Jin and received some Liao lands south of the Yin Mountains; Yelü Dashi led his followers north to Zhenzhou (Kedun City) on the steppe, gathered the seven prefectures and eighteen tribes, and planned a restoration. In the second month of 1125 Emperor Tianzuo was captured at Yingzhou by the Jin general Wanyan Loushi, and the Liao came to an end. In the tenth month Jin, citing Song's harboring of the renegade general Zhang Jue, invaded the south in eastern and western columns, and in the twelfth month Guo Yaoshi surrendered Yanshan to Jin. The Crusaders took Tyre in 1124.

1127.d: In the winter of 1125 the eastern Jin army under Wolibu broke through Yanshan and drove straight on Bianjing; Emperor Huizong of Song abdicated in favor of Qinzong. In the first month of 1126 Li Gang held Bianjing, and the Jin army withdrew north after demanding huge sums of gold and silk and the cession of the three garrison prefectures of Taiyuan, Zhongshan and Hejian. In the eighth month the Jin came south again: the western army under Nianhan took Taiyuan in the ninth month after it had held out for more than eight months, and in the intercalary eleventh month the two armies joined to take Bianjing. In the third month of 1127 the Jin carried off the emperors Huizong and Qinzong with consorts, imperial clansmen and craftsmen, more than three thousand people, to the north; the Northern Song came to an end in what is called the Jingkang Incident. In the fifth month Zhao Gou, Prince of Kang, took the throne at Yingtian Fu as Emperor Gaozong of Song and soon fell back south to Yangzhou. Song troops still held out in many cities of Hebei and Hedong. Imad al-Din Zengi took Mosul.

1130.d: In 1128–1129 the Jin army took Hebei, Hedong and Jingdong, and Emperor Gaozong of Song fled from Yangzhou to Hangzhou. In the winter of 1129 Wuzhu of Jin crossed the Yangtze and took Jiankang and Lin'an, and Gaozong took to the sea as far as Wenzhou; in the spring of 1130 Wuzhu withdrew north and was trapped at Huangtiandang near Zhenjiang by Han Shizhong's 8,000 marines for forty-eight days, escaping by cutting a channel along the Laoguan River. In the ninth month Zhang Jun gathered 400,000 men from five circuits for a decisive battle with the Jin army at Fuping, was badly beaten, and lost most of Shaanxi. In the same month Jin made Liu Yu, a Song official who had surrendered, emperor of "Great Qi", ruling Henan and Shandong; historians call it the client state of Qi. Song divided Liangzhe into East and West circuits. Zengi took Aleppo in 1128.

1134.t: Western Liao founded · Yue Fei recovers the Xiang–Han region
1134.d: Wu Jie twice defeated Wuzhu of Jin, at Heshangyuan in 1131 and at Xianren Pass in 1134, saving the gateways into Sichuan; Jin handed Shaanxi to Qi, and the Xihe prefectures were lost one after another. In 1133 Li Cheng of Qi took Xiangyang and five other prefectures, and in 1134 Yue Fei marched out and recovered them, and the fame of the Yue Family Army spread across the Yangtze and Huai. In the same year Han Shizhong's victory at Dayi beat back the invasion of the Qi and Jin allies. Yelü Dashi proclaimed himself emperor (Gurkhan) at Emil in 1132, founding the Western Liao; in 1134, at the request of the Eastern Kara-Khanids, he occupied Balasagun and made it his capital as Quz Ordu, and the Qocho Uyghurs, the Karluks and the Eastern Kara-Khanids submitted one after another.

1139.d: In 1137 Jin abolished Qi, demoted Liu Yu to Prince of Shu, and ruled his lands directly. Emperor Gaozong and Qin Gui pressed for peace, and in 1138 the capital was settled at Lin'an. In 1139 Wanyan Chang (Dalan), leader of the peace party, took charge of the Jin government and made a treaty with Song: Song would acknowledge itself a subject of Jin and pay tribute, and Jin would return the former Qi lands of Henan and Shaanxi, where Song sent officials to take over the Eastern and Western capitals and the Shaanxi circuits. The Western Liao crushed the Western Kara-Khanids at Khujand in 1137.

1141.t: Battle of Qatwan · Treaty of Shaoxing
1141.d: In 1140 Wuzhu of Jin broke the treaty, invaded the south and retook Henan and Shaanxi; Liu Qi held Shunchang, and Yue Fei crushed the Jin "flanking cavalry" at Yancheng and Yingchang and advanced to Zhuxian Town, only to be recalled by Emperor Gaozong and Qin Gui with twelve gold tablets. In 1141 Song and Jin made peace, concluding the Treaty of Shaoxing in the eleventh month: Song acknowledged itself a subject of Jin and paid an annual tribute of 250,000 each in silver and silk, the border ran down the midstream of the Huai in the east and through Dasan Pass in the west, and Song ceded the Tang and Deng prefectures and most of the Shang and Qin prefectures. In the same year Yue Fei was thrown into prison, and he was killed early the next year. In September Yelü Dashi routed the Seljuk sultan Sanjar at Qatwan north of Samarkand, and the Western Kara-Khanids and Khwarazm turned to the Western Liao as overlord. After the death of Mstislav (1132) Rus' broke up into principalities.

1154.t: Wanyan Liang moves the capital to Yanjing · Nur ad-Din unites Syria
1154.d: Wanyan Liang, the Prince of Hailing, murdered Emperor Xizong of Jin and took the throne in 1149; in 1153 he moved the capital to Yanjing, renamed it Zhongdu, and made Bianjing the Southern Capital. The steppe tribes north of the Gobi grew ever stronger, as the Keraites, Naimans, Merkits, Tatars and Mongols contended for the steppe, and the Jin court repeatedly sent troops to "reduce their numbers". Zengi took Edessa in 1144, setting off the Second Crusade (1147–1149), whose French and German kings besieged Damascus in vain; his son Nur ad-Din took Damascus in 1154 and united Muslim Syria. In 1151 Ala al-Din of the Ghurids burned and plundered Ghazni for seven days. In 1153 the Seljuk sultan Sanjar was captured by Oghuz nomads. The caliph al-Muqtafi restored real rule over Iraq.

1161.d: Sanjar died in 1157 and the east of the Great Seljuk empire fell apart: Khorasan sank into fighting among Oghuz tribes and local commanders, and Khwarazm seized the chance to expand south. The Seljuks of Iraq and of Kerman went their own ways. In 1161 Wanyan Liang tore up the treaty and invaded the south with 600,000 men in four columns, leading the main army himself to the north bank of the Yangtze; in the eleventh month Yu Yunwen took command at Caishi and crushed the Jin crossing with "sea-eel" ships; a month earlier, in the tenth month, Li Bao had burned the Jin navy with fire arrows at Tangdao off Jiaoxi. Wanyan Yong (Emperor Shizong), custodian of the Jin Eastern Capital, proclaimed himself emperor at Liaoyang; Wanyan Liang was killed by his own officers at the Guazhou ferry near Yangzhou, and the Jin army withdrew north.

1165.t: Longxing Northern Expedition · Treaty of Longxing
1165.d: In 1162 Emperor Gaozong of Song abdicated in favor of Xiaozong. Bent on recovering the north, Xiaozong recalled Zhang Jun; in 1163 Li Xianzhong and Shao Hongyuan marched north and took Lingbi, Hongxian and Suzhou, but the two generals soon fell out and their army dissolved in a single night at Fuli. In 1164 the Jin army crossed the Huai, and in 1165 the Treaty of Longxing was concluded: Song and Jin became "uncle and nephew" states, the "annual tribute" was renamed "annual payments" and reduced to 200,000 each in silver and silk, and the border remained as under the Treaty of Shaoxing. Song and Jin then kept the peace for more than forty years. Emperor Shizong of Jin governed diligently and was called "a little Yao or Shun".

1171.d: Nur ad-Din three times sent his general Shirkuh and Shirkuh's nephew Saladin into Egypt, contending for it with King Amalric of Jerusalem. In 1169 Saladin became the Fatimid vizier, and in 1171 he deposed the last caliph, al-Adid, restored the name of the Abbasid caliph in Cairo, and founded the Ayyubid dynasty, still nominally acknowledging Nur ad-Din as his master. In 1170 Goryeo had its military coup: Jeong Jung-bu and others deposed King Uijong, and the generals took power.

1176.t: Saladin unites Syria and Egypt · Myriokephalon
1176.d: Nur ad-Din died in 1174; Saladin marched north and took Damascus, and in the same year his brother Turanshah campaigned in Yemen and took control of the Hejaz. In 1175 Saladin took Homs and Hama and was invested by the caliph as sultan of Egypt and Syria, while Aleppo stayed in the hands of Zengi's heirs. In September 1176 the Byzantine emperor Manuel I marched against Rum in person and was disastrously ambushed in the pass of Myriokephalon; Byzantium never again had the strength to recover the Anatolian interior. Ghiyath al-Din of the Ghurids took Ghazni in 1173 and put his brother Muhammad in charge of it, and took Herat and Multan in 1175; the Ghaznavids fell back to the Punjab.

1187.t: Battle of Hattin · Saladin retakes Jerusalem
1187.d: Saladin took Aleppo in 1183 and received the submission of Mosul in 1185; the Islamic world was united under his banner, and the Crusader states were surrounded. At the Battle of Hattin on 4 July 1187 Saladin lured the army of King Guy of Jerusalem to the waterless Horns of Hattin and annihilated it, capturing the True Cross; from July to September Acre, Jaffa, Ascalon and the other coastal cities fell one after another, and in October Jerusalem opened its gates and surrendered, leaving the Crusaders only Tyre, Tripoli and Antioch. In 1185 the Asen brothers of Bulgaria rose against Byzantium and founded the Second Bulgarian Empire. In 1186 the Ghurids took Lahore and the Ghaznavids came to an end. Rum annexed the Danishmendids in 1178. In Japan the Taira were destroyed in the Battle of Dan-no-ura in 1185.

1194.t: Khwarazm destroys the Seljuks · Yellow River captures the Huai
1194.d: The Third Crusade (1189–1192): the German emperor Frederick I drowned in the Saleph River in Cilicia; King Richard of England and King Philip II of France took Acre in 1191, Richard defeated Saladin at Arsuf, and in 1192 the two sides made the Treaty of Jaffa, under which the Crusaders kept the coast from Tyre to Jaffa and Christians could make pilgrimage to Jerusalem; on the way Richard seized Cyprus. Saladin died in 1193. In 1192 Muhammad of Ghor defeated the coalition of Rajput kings at the second Battle of Tarain and took Delhi the next year. In 1194 Tekish, Shah of Khwarazm, killed Tughril III, the last sultan of the Seljuks of Iraq, at Rayy. In the same year the Yellow River broke its banks at Yangwu and its main current turned south, capturing the Huai on its way to the sea. In 1192 Minamoto no Yoritomo became shogun and founded the Kamakura shogunate.

1204.t: Temüjin unites the steppe · Fourth Crusade
1204.d: Temüjin of the Kiyad, allied with the Ong Khan of the Keraites, helped Jin defeat the Tatars in 1196; he destroyed the Tatars in 1202, surprised the Ong Khan at the Jeje'er Heights in 1203 and ended the Keraites, and in 1204 crushed Tayang Khan of the Naimans at Naqu Cliff while the Merkits too were routed, so that all the tribes north of the Gobi came under Temüjin. In April of the same year the Fourth Crusade, steered by Venice, took Constantinople, plundered it and founded the Latin Empire; Byzantine nobles set up rival courts at Nicaea and Trebizond. The Ghurids took Kannauj in 1194, and in 1203–1204 their general Bakhtiyar Khalji broke into Bengal. Queen Tamar of Georgia took Ani and Kars.

1206.t: Founding of the Mongol Empire · Kaixi Northern Expedition
1206.d: In 1206 Temüjin held a kurultai at the source of the Onon, was proclaimed Genghis Khan and founded the Great Mongol State, organizing his people into ninety-five units of a thousand households. The Mongols had made their first attack on Western Xia in 1205. Under Emperor Ningzong of Song, Han Tuozhou pressed for a northern expedition, and in the fifth month of 1206 Song declared war on Jin; its attacks on Suzhou, Tangzhou and Caizhou all failed, and the Jin army counterattacked in Huainan and at Xiangyang. Wu Xi, deputy pacification commissioner of Sichuan, secretly went over to Jin, took the title King of Shu the next year, and was soon killed. Muhammad of Ghor was assassinated in 1206, and his Turkish slave commander Aybak made himself independent at Delhi, founding the Delhi Sultanate. Byzantine nobles set up another regime in Epirus, and the Bulgarian tsar Kaloyan captured the Latin emperor Baldwin at Adrianople (1205).

1210.t: Mongols attack Xia · The Uyghurs submit
1210.d: In 1207 Jochi campaigned north against the "Forest Peoples", and the Oirats, the Kyrgyz and other tribes submitted. In 1209 Barchuq, idiqut of the Qocho Uyghurs, killed the Western Liao resident official and sent envoys to submit to Genghis Khan. In the same year Genghis Khan invaded Western Xia for the third time, broke through Keyimen, besieged Zhongxing Fu and diverted the Yellow River to flood the city; in 1210 Emperor Xiangzong of Xia gave him a daughter in marriage, sued for peace and acknowledged himself a Mongol subject. Muhammad II, Shah of Khwarazm, broke away from the Western Liao and in 1210 defeated the Western Liao army near Talas; the remnant Ghurid regime submitted to Khwarazm. The Sultanate of Rum took Antalya in 1207, opening an outlet to the Mediterranean.

1212.t: Battle of Yehuling · Kuchlug usurps the Western Liao
1212.d: In 1211 Genghis Khan attacked Jin in force; in the eighth month he wiped out the main Jin army of 400,000 at Yehuling and Huihebao and closed in on Zhongdu, and in 1212 Jebe briefly broke into the Eastern Capital, Liaoyang Fu. The Khitan Yelü Liuge rose at Long'an and Hanzhou and joined the Mongols. Arslan Khan, chief of the Karluks, and the lord of Almaliq submitted to the Mongols. In the Western Liao the Naiman prince Kuchlug, whom the Gurkhan Zhilugu had taken in, usurped the throne; Kuchlug soon seized Kashgar, ending the Eastern Kara-Khanids. In 1212 Muhammad II of Khwarazm stormed Samarkand, killed Uthman, the last Western Kara-Khanid ruler, and took all Transoxiana.

1215.t: Fall of Zhongdu · Jin moves the capital to Bianjing
1215.d: In 1213–1214 three Mongol armies swept through more than ninety commanderies of Hebei, Hedong and Shandong; Emperor Xuanzong of Jin offered the Princess of Qi to sue for peace and then, in the fifth month of 1214, moved the capital to Bianjing. Zhongdu fell in the fifth month of 1215, and the Mongols held all of the Yan and Yun lands and Liaoxi. Puxian Wannu, Jin pacification commissioner of Liaodong, rebelled against Jin and founded the state of Great Zhen (Eastern Xia). In the same year Khwarazm took Ghazni and the Ghurid dynasty ended; Sinop passed to the Sultanate of Rum.

1218.t: Jebe destroys the Western Liao · Otrar incident
1218.d: In 1217 Genghis Khan made Muqali Grand Preceptor and Prince of the State to direct the conquest of North China; the next year Muqali took Taiyuan and other prefectures of Hedong. In 1218 Jebe attacked the Western Liao with 20,000 horsemen; deserted by his people, Kuchlug fled to Badakhshan, where he was caught and killed. The Western Liao ended, and all eastern Turkestan passed to the Mongols. Puxian Wannu of Eastern Xia moved east to the Helan Circuit and held the lands east of the Jin Supreme Capital; Yelü Liuge, allied with the Mongols, held Liaodong. In the same year Inalchuq, the Khwarazmian governor of Otrar, killed a Mongol caravan of more than four hundred men as spies; when Genghis Khan sent envoys to demand redress, they too were killed, and the western campaign began. Goryeo and the Mongols jointly besieged the Khitan remnants who had fled into Gangdong Fortress. The Fifth Crusade landed in Egypt.

1220.d: In the autumn of 1219 Genghis Khan led a great army west in person. He left Chagatai and Ögedei to besiege Otrar, sent Jochi down the Syr Darya, and led the main army straight to Bukhara. Bukhara fell in February 1220 and Samarkand surrendered in March; Muhammad II of Khwarazm fled west with Jebe and Subutai in relentless pursuit, and at the end of the year died of illness on the island of Abeskun in the Caspian. Muqali took Zhending, and Yan Shi of Dongping in Shandong surrendered his forces to the Mongols. Li Quan and Peng Yibin of the Red Coat army in eastern Shandong went over to the Southern Song. The Fifth Crusade took Damietta in Egypt.

1221.d: In the spring of 1221 the Mongols took the old Khwarazmian capital, Gurganj, and diverted the Amu Darya to flood it; Tolui massacred Merv, Nishapur and Herat, and the cities of Khorasan were almost all destroyed; Mö'etüken, son of Chagatai, was killed at Bamiyan, and Genghis Khan ordered the city massacred. Jalal al-Din defeated Shigi Qutuqu at Parwan, but in November of the same year Genghis Khan caught him on the bank of the Indus and destroyed his army; Jalal al-Din leapt his horse into the river and escaped to India. The Fifth Crusade was checked at Mansurah and gave back Damietta.

1223.d: After their pursuit of Muhammad, Jebe and Subutai pressed on west, twice defeated the Georgian army in 1221, crossed the Caucasus in 1222 and defeated the Alans and Kipchaks, and in May 1223 routed the Rus'–Kipchak allies at the Kalka River north of the Sea of Azov, capturing and killing Grand Prince Mstislav III of Kyiv; on their way back they were ambushed by the Bulgars on the middle Volga and returned east by a roundabout route. Muqali, after seven years directing the war in North China, died at Wenxi in Shanxi in 1223. Western Xia refused to send troops for the western campaign, and Mongol–Xia relations broke down. Emperor Xuanzong of Jin died and Aizong took the throne.

1227.t: Fall of Western Xia · Death of Genghis Khan
1227.d: Genghis Khan returned east in 1225 and gave his sons their appanages: Jochi received the lands west of the Irtysh and north of Khwarazm, Chagatai the Ili, Semirechye and Transoxiana, Ögedei Emil and Qobuq, while Tolui kept the Mongol homeland. In 1226 the Mongols, citing Western Xia's refusal to send troops, attacked in force, took the Gan, Su and Liang prefectures, and crushed the Xia relief army at the "nine crossings of the Yellow River"; in 1227 they besieged Zhongxing Fu. In the seventh month Genghis Khan died of illness in Qingshui County below the Liupan Mountains, ordering that his death be kept secret; the last Xia ruler came out to surrender and was killed, and Western Xia came to an end. Li Quan surrendered Shandong to the Mongols. Jalal al-Din returned to Iran in 1225, destroyed the Eldiguzids of Azerbaijan and defeated the Georgian army at Garni. In Đại Việt the Trần replaced the Lý (1225).

1232.t: Battle of Sanfengshan · Fall of Jalal al-Din
1232.d: Ögedei took the throne as Great Khan in 1229 and marched against Jin in person in 1230, sending Tolui through Song territory at Hanzhong to come out on the Jin army's flank and rear. In the first month of 1232, in heavy snow at Sanfengshan in Junzhou, Tolui wiped out the main Jin army of 150,000; the famous Jin generals Wanyan Heda and Yila Pu'a were killed, and the Mongols then besieged Bianjing. Chormaqan entered Iran with 30,000 horsemen in 1230; Jalal al-Din was killed in the Kurdish mountains in 1231, Khwarazm came to an end, and Azerbaijan and Arran passed to the Mongols. The Mongols made their first full-scale invasion of Goryeo in 1231, and the next year Goryeo moved its capital to Ganghwa Island. Kayqubad, sultan of Rum, defeated Jalal al-Din at Yassıçemen in 1230. In 1229 the Holy Roman Emperor Frederick II recovered Jerusalem from Egypt by negotiation.

1234.t: Siege of Caizhou · Fall of the Jin
1234.d: In 1233 Cui Li, commander at Bianjing, surrendered to the Mongols, and Emperor Aizong of Jin fled to Guide and then Caizhou. Song allied with the Mongols, and the Song general Meng Gong brought 20,000 men and 300,000 shi of grain to help the Mongol Tachar besiege Caizhou. The city fell in the first month of 1234; Aizong abdicated to his clansman Chenglin and hanged himself, Chenglin was killed in the fighting, and the Jin came to an end. Song gained the Tang, Deng and Cai prefectures. In the sixth month of the same year, as the Mongols withdrew north, Emperor Lizong of Song ordered Zhao Kui and Quan Zicai to recover the three capitals; the Song armies entered Bianjing and Luoyang but, with their supplies failing, were routed by the Mongols. This "Duanping entry into Luoyang" began the Song–Mongol war. The Mongol prince Güyük destroyed Eastern Xia in 1233.

1236.t: The eldest sons' western campaign · Mongols break into Sichuan
1236.d: In 1235 Ögedei built the city of Karakorum by the Orkhon and decided to send out three armies: Batu was to lead the eldest sons of the princes west against the Kipchaks and Rus', Köten to attack Sichuan, and Köchü to attack Jingxiang. In 1236 the garrison of Xiangyang mutinied and surrendered, and the prefectures of the Jingxi South Circuit were lost one after another; in the tenth month Köten took Chengdu, massacred its people and withdrew, leaving western Sichuan in ruins. In the autumn of the same year Batu and Subutai destroyed Volga Bulgaria. Chormaqan subdued Georgia, and Queen Rusudan fled to Kutaisi.

1238.d: In the autumn of 1237 Batu defeated Bachman, a Kipchak chief on the lower Volga, and in December, braving the bitter cold, stormed Ryazan, where the inhabitants were wiped out; he went on to take Kolomna and Moscow, took Vladimir in February 1238, and in March wiped out the army of Grand Prince Yuri II of Vladimir on the Sit River. On their way south the Mongols met seven weeks of stubborn resistance at the small town of Kozelsk, which they massacred and called the "evil city". Seven or eight in ten of the cities of northeastern Rus' were destroyed. The Mongols took Isfahan in 1237.

1241.d: In 1239 the Mongols took Chernihiv and Pereiaslav and destroyed Magas, the capital of the Alans; the Kipchak chief Köten fled into Hungary with forty thousand tents. Kyiv fell in December 1240. In 1241 Batu divided his forces: Baidar and Qadan led the northern column into Poland, burned Kraków in March, and on 9 April crushed the Polish–German army of Duke Henry II of Silesia at Legnica; on 11 April the main army under Batu and Subutai routed King Béla IV of Hungary at Mohi on the Sajó, a tributary of the Tisza, and then crossed the Danube. Ögedei died at Karakorum at the end of the year. The Song general Meng Gong recovered Xiangyang in 1239.

1243.t: Battle of Köse Dağ · Batu founds Sarai
1243.d: In the spring of 1242 news of Ögedei's death arrived; Batu withdrew from Hungary and returned east by way of Bulgaria, which then paid tribute to the Mongols. Batu built Sarai on the lower Volga as his capital, and the Rus' princes had to go there to pay homage and receive their patents; Novgorod also paid tribute. In the same year Alexander Nevsky of Novgorod crushed the Teutonic Order on the ice of Lake Peipus. In June 1243 Baiju routed Kaykhusraw II, sultan of Rum, at Köse Dağ northeast of Sivas, and Rum, Trebizond, Cilician Armenia and Mosul submitted to the Mongols one after another.

1250.t: Mamluks replace the Ayyubids · Liangzhou meeting
1250.d: In 1244 the remnants of the Khwarazmian army, driven out of Iran by the Mongols, took Jerusalem at Egypt's invitation, and in the same year, with the Egyptian army, annihilated the Crusaders at La Forbie near Gaza. King Louis IX of France launched the Seventh Crusade, took Damietta in 1249, and in February 1250 was defeated at Mansurah by the Mamluk guard and captured; in May the Mamluks killed the Ayyubid sultan Turanshah and seized Egypt. In 1247 Sakya Pandita, leader of the Sakya school of Tibet, met Köten at Liangzhou, and Tibet submitted to the Mongols. The Empire of Nicaea took Thessalonica in 1246.

1253.d: In 1251 Möngke, son of Tolui, took the throne as Great Khan with Batu's support, purged the lines of Ögedei and Chagatai, put Kublai in charge of the Chinese lands south of the Gobi, and sent Hulagu west. In the autumn of 1253 Kublai led an army south from Lintao along the eastern edge of Tibet, crossed the Jinsha River "on skin rafts", and in the twelfth month took Yangjumie City, capital of the Dali kingdom; the next year King Duan Xingzhi was captured and Dali came to an end, and Uriyangkhadai was left in command. The Song general Yu Jie organized the defense of Sichuan by building fortified towns on the mountains; Diaoyu Fortress and seven others formed the "eight pillars" of this mountain-fortress system.

1256.d: Hulagu set out west in 1253, entered Iran in 1256 and besieged the Nizari castles; in November the last Nizari imam, Rukn al-Din, surrendered at Maymun-Diz, and Alamut and more than a hundred other mountain castles fell one after another; only Girdkuh held out, until 1270. The Amu Darya Branch Secretariat was absorbed into Hulagu's ulus. Kublai built Kaiping Fu on the upper Luan River in 1256. Batu died in 1255; Sartaq and then Ulaghchi succeeded him, both dying young, and in 1257 Batu's brother Berke took the throne.

1258.t: Fall of Baghdad · Möngke invades Sichuan
1258.d: In January 1258 Hulagu joined Baiju's army to surround Baghdad; the city fell on 10 February and was plundered and massacred for weeks, and the last caliph, al-Musta'sim, was rolled in a carpet and trampled to death by horses; the Abbasid dynasty, more than five hundred years old, came to an end. In the same year Möngke attacked Song in three columns: he led the main army into Sichuan himself, taking Kuzhu Pass at Jianmen, Langzhou, Pengzhou, Guang'an and other cities one after another; Kublai attacked Ezhou, and Uriyangkhadai marched north from Yunnan by way of Đại Việt. Uriyangkhadai had broken into Thăng Long in the winter of 1257. The Choe regime in Goryeo was overthrown, and the Mongols set up the Ssangseong Command in its northeast.

1259.d: From the second month of 1259 Möngke attacked Diaoyu Fortress in Hezhou in person; its commanders Wang Jian and Zhang Jue held the strong position for five months, and in the seventh month Möngke died of illness before the walls (or, some say, of wounds from a catapult stone), and the Mongol armies attacking Sichuan withdrew north. In the ninth month Kublai crossed the Yangtze and besieged Ezhou; Jia Sidao sent envoys to sue for peace, offering to cede the land north of the river and make annual payments. In the eleventh month, hearing that his younger brother Ariq Böke meant to take the throne at Karakorum, Kublai went back north to contend for the succession. Wang Jeon, crown prince of Goryeo, came to the Mongol court to surrender, and Goryeo submitted to the Mongols.

1260.d: In the third month of 1260 Kublai took the throne as khan at Kaiping with the reign title Zhongtong; in the fourth month Ariq Böke proclaimed himself khan at Karakorum, and the Mongol Empire fell into civil war. The western princes went their own ways: Berke's Golden Horde, Hulagu's Ilkhanate and Alghu's Chagatai Khanate became states of their own from then on. Early in the year Hulagu took Aleppo and Damascus, ending the Ayyubid regime in Syria; on news of Möngke's death he led his main army back east, leaving Kitbuqa to hold Syria. On 3 September the Mamluk sultan Qutuz and Baybars annihilated Kitbuqa's army at Ain Jalut in Palestine; the Mongol advance west was stopped, and Syria passed to the Mamluks.

1264.d: In 1261 Kublai defeated Ariq Böke at Shimultai Lake; Ariq Böke withdrew west to the Ili valley and, his cause exhausted, surrendered in 1264. In 1262 Li Tan, hereditary warlord of Shandong, rebelled against the Yuan and went over to Song; besieged at Jinan, he was defeated and killed, and from then on Kublai stripped the Chinese hereditary warlords of their troops. Kaiping was raised to Shangdu in 1263 and Yanjing renamed Zhongdu in 1264, and the Supreme Control Commission was set up under Phagpa to administer Tibetan affairs. In 1261 Michael VIII of Nicaea recovered Constantinople, the Latin Empire came to an end, and Byzantium was restored. Berke of the Golden Horde and Hulagu of the Ilkhanate fought on the Terek River over Azerbaijan (1262–1263).

1269.d: Kaidu, grandson of Ögedei, rebuilt the power of the Ögedeid line from Emil, and in 1269 met Baraq, khan of the Chagatai, and Möngke Temür, khan of the Golden Horde, at Talas; they divided Transoxiana among themselves and formed an alliance against the Yuan, and the Yuan's northwestern frontier knew no peace from then on. In 1268 the Yuan general Aju and the Song defector Liu Zheng began the siege of Xiangyang and Fancheng, which the Song general Lü Wenhuan held to the last. In the same year the Mamluk sultan Baybars took Antioch, ending the Principality of Antioch. In 1266 the Mamluks crushed Cilician Armenia at Mari and burned and plundered Sis.

1273.t: Fall of Xiangyang · The Great Yuan proclaimed
1273.d: In 1270 King Wonjong of Goryeo returned to Gaegyeong, and the Yuan set up Dongning Fu at Pyongyang, the Western Capital; the defiant Sambyeolcho fell back to Jindo and Jeju and were suppressed by the Yuan–Goryeo allies in 1273. In 1271 Kublai took the dynastic name Great Yuan from the words "Great indeed is the Primal Qian" in the Book of Changes, and the next year Zhongdu was renamed Dadu. In the first month of 1273 the Yuan army breached Fancheng with Muslim counterweight trebuchets, and in the second month Lü Wenhuan surrendered Xiangyang to the Yuan, leaving the Song gateway on the middle Yangtze wide open. In 1271 the Mamluks took Krak des Chevaliers.

1274.t: Bayan crosses the Yangtze · First Mongol invasion of Japan
1274.d: In 1274 the Yuan put Bayan in command of an army of 200,000, which went down the Han, bypassed Yingzhou, and in the twelfth month forced a crossing of the Yangtze at Yangluo; Ezhou surrendered in the first month of the next year. In the tenth month of the same year a Yuan–Goryeo force of more than 30,000 sailed from Happo, attacked Tsushima and Iki and landed at Hakata Bay; after fierce fighting with the Japanese warriors it withdrew to its ships at night, met a storm, suffered heavy losses and went home. The Japanese call it the Bun'ei campaign. Sayyid Ajjal Shams al-Din set up Yunnan Province, with its seat at Zhongqing.

1276.d: In 1275 Jia Sidao met the Yuan at Dingjiazhou with 130,000 Song troops, which broke at the first clash; the Yuan army went on down the river to take Jiangzhou, Anqing, Jiankang and Zhenjiang, and in the eleventh month massacred Changzhou. In the first month of 1276 Empress Dowager Xie presented the imperial seal and surrendered; in the third month Bayan entered Lin'an and carried off Emperor Gong and the empress dowager to the north. Lu Xiufu and Zhang Shijie enthroned Zhao Shi, Prince of Yi, at Fuzhou (Emperor Duanzong); at the end of the year Fuzhou and Quanzhou were lost, Pu Shougeng surrendered Quanzhou to the Yuan, and the Song court took to the sea in exile. Li Tingzhi held Yangzhou until it fell in the seventh month and he was killed. In the southwest, Diaoyu Fortress, Chongqing, Kuizhou and other places were still in Song hands.

1279.t: Battle of Yamen · Yuan unifies China
1279.d: In 1278 Emperor Duanzong of Song died of illness at Naozhou, and Lu Xiufu and Zhang Shijie enthroned his younger brother Zhao Bing and moved to Yashan at Xinhui in Guangdong. In the second month of 1279 the Yuan general Zhang Hongfan attacked Yashan with his fleet; the Song fleet of more than a thousand ships, lashed together, collapsed after being cut off from water for over ten days, and Lu Xiufu leapt into the sea with the eight-year-old emperor on his back; the Song came to an end. In the same year Wang Li, commander of Diaoyu Fortress, opened its gates to the Yuan, and all of Sichuan passed to the Yuan. The Yuan realm was now larger than any before it, "beyond the Yin Mountains in the north, to the Flowing Sands in the west, to the end of Liaodong in the east, and beyond the seas in the south"; in the west the Golden Horde, the Chagatai and the Ilkhanate, and Kaidu, nominally acknowledged the Yuan as overlord but in fact went their own ways. In 1277 the Yuan army crushed the Burmese army of Pagan at Ngasaunggyan on the Yunnan frontier.
